reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.updateEntity(slot, { group }) — an OIMIndex over `group` re-files the row
reading.floor: delete from the old Set, store the column, add to the new Set
reading.caveat: THE INDEX IS AUTOMATIC AGAIN, SO THIS IS THE ORIGINAL QUESTION. `OIMIndex` hears its source collection through a content-change listener: `updateEntity` marks the row, the listener reads the key the row was last filed under from the row's own `indexKeys` cell, compares it with `keyOf(entity)` and moves the slot with `removeBucketMemberSlotByKey` + `addBucketMemberSlotByKey`. The caller writes one column and nothing else. All sixty-four buckets are held before the clock, because an index files only into buckets that exist. A reading recorded under this id while the move was the caller's (`removeSlotAt` + `appendSlot` on a positional bucket collection) priced a different body and must not be quoted against this one. WHERE THE TWO SIDES ARE NOT DOING THE SAME WORK. Ours resolves BOTH buckets by key through the bucket store (two `Map.get`), as the floor resolves both `Set`s; the unordered bucket is a `Set`, so leave and join are hashes on both sides. Ours additionally reads and writes the row's index cell, holds and unholds the row from the buckets, queues both buckets for the change-close flush that marks them on the channel so a subscriber can be woken, and marks the row itself — and the flush that closes the batch is inside the timed body. The floor can be read by iterating it and by nothing else. Direction: inflates our ratio.

reading.ours: collection.clearContent(slot) — through the identity, no index registered
reading.caveat: THE HASH IS ON THE FLOOR'S SIDE ONLY: ours is handed the identity and the floor hashes a string, which flatters us — the deleteEntityByKey path is not priced here and would cost us that lookup too. Against that, ours clears the value through the writer, reports it on the channel, recomputes emptiness and asks whether anything holds or references the identity before it unfiles it from the store — an unheld, emptied slot is released at the call. The flush that closes the batch is inside the timed body. The floor's row is gone the instant delete returns and nothing can be subscribed to it. Both sides rebuild their population between passes, untimed.

reading.floor: map.delete(id) and Set.delete(row) from the group it was in
reading.caveat: Ours finds the bucket to leave through the key the row's own `indexKeys` cell carries — one cell read and one bucket-store `Map.get` — where the floor hashes the id and then hashes the group name. Against that, ours clears the value, tells the index through its content listener, unholds the row from the bucket, queues the bucket for the change-close flush that marks it on the channel, and unfiles the emptied identity; the flush that closes this batch is inside the timed body. The buckets are held for the whole pass, so none is released under the clock. The floor leaves an empty Set behind for ever and tells nobody.

reading.ours: collection.findEntityByKey(id) — the entity of a key, or undefined
reading.caveat: THE CALIBRATION ROW. `findEntityByKey` is `findSlotByKey` — one call into the slot store service and one `Map.get` — and one `.entity` load off the slot, so if this reads much above 1 the instrument is measuring call overhead rather than the library, and every other ratio in this table should be read with that in mind. Every key hits — a miss is a different path on both sides and would mix two prices.

reading.ours: collection.holdSlotByKey(id) — resolve a key to an identity and keep it, minting on a miss
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR CANNOT MINT AND CANNOT KEEP, and those are the two differences. `holdSlotByKey` promises an identity for a key the population has never seen, so a caller can subscribe to a row before it arrives; and the hold is a COUNTED REFERENCE, so nothing can unfile that identity while the caller still has it. Every key here HITS, so the minting branch never runs — what is left over the map read is the store call, the `=== undefined` compare that is false on every hit, and one `holdCount++` (`OIMSlotAggregate.holdSlotByKey` into `OIMSlotOwner.holdSlot`). THE TWO ALLOCATIONS THIS CAVEAT CHARGED NO LONGER EXIST AND NOTHING REPLACES THEM. It read "TWO ALLOCATIONS PER CALL: the `{ slot, release }` record and the release closure `holdSlot` builds", and that was the charge the row was built to expose: a minting door that allocated where a `Map.get` does not. No door hands back such a record — `holdSlotByKey` returns the slot and increments one field — so the hit path allocates nothing on either side and what is left between the two columns is one call and one store. Direction: inflates our ratio, now by the store call and the increment alone. READ IT AGAINST `find.vs-map-get` DIRECTLY ABOVE — the gap between the two is what the minting door costs over the reading one, on the hit path, and that gap is the whole reason the documentation says to hold an identity rather than resolve it per read. THIS BODY NEVER GIVES THE HOLD BACK. The door is `OIMEntityCollection.releaseSlotIfUnheld` and nothing here calls it, so the hold count grows for the life of the process — one decrement per call that we do not charge ourselves for, and it is the only item on this row that runs in our favour. This row measures a minting HOLD.

reading.ours: slot.entity — the row behind an identity you already hold
reading.caveat: ONE INDIRECTION AGAINST NONE, which is the smallest thing this table can ask about and is close to the resolution floor — read it against the control rows before treating any part of it as a result. Ours answers `TPriceDataRow | undefined` because an identity may carry no value; the floor answers a row. This body does NOT narrow the undefined, so the branch a real consumer writes is charged to neither side. IT IS THE WHOLE VALUE-READ PATH NOW. `value.held-getValue-vs-object` and `value.construct-and-read-vs-object` stood below this row and priced the same read through an observable; there is no observable, so this is the only shape the question has left.

reading.ours: byGroup.buckets.find(address) — the bucket at an address, or nothing
reading.caveat: THE ADDRESS LOOKUP ON THE BUCKET SIDE, WITHOUT THE HOLD, so a reader can see which part of `hold.vs-map-get` is the store call and which part is the minting and the two allocations. Every address here hits and `find` cannot mint, so ours is one field load, one call and one `Map.get` against the floor's one `Map.get`. Both sides cycle through all sixty-four addresses. `OIMSlotByKeyStoreMapDriven` holds one `Map` and nothing else, so there is no cell to hit or miss.

reading.ours: for (const slot of byGroup.read(bucket)) slot.entity — per member visited
reading.floor: for (const row of set) — per member visited, same container kind
reading.caveat: THE SAME CONTAINER ON BOTH SIDES: an unordered bucket holds its members in a `Set`, so this floor is the structural equal. Ours pays two things the floor does not — the read settles whatever order report is outstanding on the bucket (nothing is outstanding here, and an unordered bucket has no order to settle, so what is charged is the ASKING) and every member is a slot the consumer must dereference to reach the row, which this body does. The per-read costs — the settle and the iterator — are amortised over the hundred-odd members of a bucket, so a caller reading buckets of one pays far more per member than this row shows.

reading.ours: for (const slot of byGroup.read(bucket)) slot.entity — per member visited
reading.floor: for (let i = 0; i < rows.length; i++) — per member visited
reading.caveat: THE SAME OUR-SIDE BODY AS THE ROW ABOVE AGAINST THE FLOOR SOMEBODY WOULD ACTUALLY WRITE. An indexed array walk is the fastest way there is to visit a hundred objects and it beats a `Set` iterator handily, so this ratio is the worse of the two and the more honest answer to "what does reading a group cost me". What the array cannot do is stay correct: nothing maintains it, nothing can be woken by it, and it holds rows rather than identities that outlive them. The gap between this ratio and the `set-iteration` one above is a property of JavaScript containers, not of either design.

Ours is two calls deep — the bucket collection hands the question to its bucket slots service, whose `size` reads the same `Set.size` — and those two calls are the whole difference. The floor reads a field of a container whose correctness is somebody else's problem. Both sides cycle through all sixty-four buckets rather than asking the same one repeatedly. THIS ROW ONCE READ BELOW 1.00 AND THAT NUMBER WAS A HASH, NOT A COUNT. The floor reached its `Set` through `sets.get(name)` — a string-keyed `Map.get` — while our side was handed the bucket out of an array. So the floor's number was very nearly all addressing and ours was very nearly all service hop, and the row reported the difference between a hash and an array load under the name of a member count. The floor now holds its sets in an array indexed exactly the way our side indexes its buckets, so both sides are addressed alike and what is left in the ratio is the service hop. This suite's standing rule is that a floor doing less is a lie in our favour; that rule was pointed at us here, and the reading it produced is withdrawn rather than qualified. THE CALL WAS `db.memberCount(bucket)` AND IS `bucketCollection.getBucketMemberSlotCount(bucket)`, on the bucket collection rather than on the database — the same question through a different object. Nothing recorded before 2026-08-29 is re-attributed to it, and the prediction the old caveat carried (roughly 3.5 to 4.4, from figures in `measurements/2026-08-20-price/read-2`) was written for the old call and is not a prediction about this one.

reading.ours: channel.flush() with nothing marked and nobody subscribed
reading.floor: a call that bumps a frame counter
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR HERE IS ESSENTIALLY ZERO AND THE RATIO IS THEREFORE NOT A READING — take the absolute nanoseconds on our side and ignore the multiple. A hand-written store has no frame to close, so the nearest thing to a floor is the bookkeeping a person writes instead, and V8 inlines that to almost nothing. What ours does for the money: runs the effect graph's drain, swaps the two delivery lists, walks an empty delivery, runs the after-flush and after-each-frame phases, sweeps identities nobody holds and reports errors. This number is the fixed cost every other frame row carries, which is what makes it worth printing even though its ratio means nothing. AND THE MULTIPLE IS NOT THE ONLY THING TO IGNORE HERE: the floor is timed twice around our side and the two timings disagree by more than the gap they bracket, which is what the noise column on this row says. The absolute figure on our side is the reading; it is split by `flush.empty-vs-the-same-bookkeeping-by-hand`, whose floor performs these same phases inline.

reading.ours: channel.flush() with nothing marked and nobody subscribed
reading.floor: the same phases written out inline over a plain object: the two guards, the before-flush test, the empty leaf walk, the two emptiness tests and the counter
reading.caveat: THIS ROW EXISTS TO SPLIT `flush.empty-vs-noop`, WHICH IS A PRICE AGAINST NOTHING. That row puts an empty frame against a counter bump, so its multiple prices the existence of a frame rather than anything inside one, and it cannot say which part of the absolute figure is the bookkeeping and which is the SHAPE the bookkeeping is written in. This floor does the same work: the same field reads, the same stores, the same walk of an empty leaf array, the same two emptiness tests — the after-each-frame set and the error list — and the same frame-counter increment, over a plain object with no methods. THE FLOOR WAS RE-TRANSCRIBED and it is a SHORTER body than the one this row was first measured with. It used to write out the two-list delivery swap, the levelled scheduler drain, the release sweep, the deferred-callback queue and the bound on the spare list, because `OIMDB.runFrame` did all five. `OIMChannel.runFrame` does none of them: a frame is one pass over one flat `leaves` array, then `dispatchAfterEachFrame`, then `reportErrors`. Keeping the old phases would have made this floor do MORE than the engine, which is the one direction a floor may never drift in — so nothing recorded against this id is a like-for-like continuation of what it measures now, and no earlier figure is re-attributed to it. WHAT IS LEFT IN THE RATIO: the call frames our side enters (`flush`, `runFrame`, `dispatchAfterEachFrame`, `reportErrors`), the two `try`/`finally` regions, the `do`/`while` a single frame still goes round once, and the difference between a class field and a property of an object literal. A reading at 1.00 says the phases ARE the price and nothing can come off without dropping a phase; a reading above it says the structure is worth attacking and names its size. Direction: this floor does MORE than any floor in this file — it is our own design transcribed — so the ratio understates our cost against a primitive and is not comparable with the rows around it. It is a decomposition instrument and not a price.

reading.ours: update the row, flush, and the subscription fires — per identity delivered
reading.floor: store the field and call the handler — per row
reading.caveat: ONE WRITE PER IDENTITY PER FRAME, WHICH IS THE WORST CASE FOR US. Both sides call the handler exactly once per row, so nothing here is saved by coalescing — the mechanism ours pays for on every write is deliberately given nothing to do. Ours per operation: the whole update path, then the stamp, then the enlisting of every effect on the slot onto the frame's leaf array, then the frame walking that array and running each body. The floor: one store and one call. The fixed cost of the frame itself is divided by a thousand deliveries here; `flush.empty-vs-noop` prices it directly so a reader can subtract it. What ours buys and the floor cannot: the handler is registered against the identity, so a writer does not have to know who is listening. A SUBSCRIPTION IS AN EFFECT NOW and that is not only a renaming: `effectService.createEffect` allocates a `TOIMEffect` that keeps its own root list, and the give-back is `effect.detach()` rather than a disposer closure.

reading.ours: effectService.createEffect([column slot of 'title'], [], h) — the narrowest signal the engine has
reading.floor: store the field and call h only when the name that moved is 'title'
reading.caveat: THE ONE COLUMN THAT MOVED IS THE ONE SUBSCRIBED TO, on both sides, so this is the happy case. THE MECHANISM UNDER OURS CHANGED AND THE OLD CAVEAT DESCRIBED THE OTHER ONE. It said the write records a per-identity list of moved column names and the handler consults that list on delivery, so two field subscriptions on one identity both woke and one returned having found its name absent. There is no such list and no such filter: a COLUMN OF A ROW IS ITS OWN IDENTITY, minted by `holdColumn` and hanging on the row, and a write marks only the column slots that exist. So a `note` write does not reach a `title` subscriber at all. The figure the old sentence stood behind is not re-attributed to this shape, and nothing recorded against this id is a like-for-like continuation of it. WHAT IS LEFT IN THE RATIO: the mint is outside the clock (one per row, at build), and inside it ours pays the write path, the column mark, the enlist and the frame, against the floor's one store and one string compare.
